3470:
To contrive something means to plan, create, or bring something about through deliberate, clever thinking — especially when conditions are difficult, resources are limited, or the method involves some calculation and effort.

The key feeling inside the word is this: things did not happen by accident, naturally, or easily. Someone worked their mind to make it happen. There is always a sense of deliberate human effort and ingenuity behind it.

"Contrive" does not have just one meaning. It has three closely related senses that you need to understand separately.

Sense 1 — To cleverly devise or invent something

This is the most common use. You use your intelligence to think up a plan, method, or solution — often when it isn't obvious how to proceed.

  • She contrived a way to sneak out of the house without waking anyone.
  • With only a rope and a broken ladder, he contrived a way to reach the window.
  • The general contrived a strategy that nobody had expected.

In this sense, "contrive" is close to "devise" or "think up cleverly." It often implies working with whatever is available, finding a way where there didn't seem to be one.

Sense 2 — To manage to do something, but with effort (or barely)

Here, "contrive" means that someone succeeded in doing something, but the phrasing hints that it wasn't easy, wasn't natural, or perhaps happened through questionable means.

  • Despite being furious, she contrived to remain calm throughout the meeting.
  • He contrived to arrive on time, though nobody understood how.
  • They contrived to finish the project just before the deadline.

A useful test: if you can replace "contrived to" with "somehow managed to," you are probably in this territory. There is often a quiet undertone of "it took real effort" or even "it was a near thing."

Sense 3 — To secretly scheme or plot something

"Contrive" can also carry a clearly negative meaning — to plan something sneaky, manipulative, or deceptive.

  • He contrived a false story to make himself look innocent.
  • She contrived a situation where her rival would be publicly embarrassed.
  • The minister contrived a way to shift the blame onto his colleagues.

Here, the word overlaps with "scheme" or "plot." The cleverness has gone sour — it is being used for selfish or dishonest ends.
The Tone: When Is It Positive, Neutral, or Negative?

This is the most important thing to understand about "contrive," because the word lives on a sliding scale.

On one end, it can sound admirable — someone is being resourceful and smart, finding solutions against the odds. A wartime inventor contriving a weapon from scrap parts, or a chef contriving a delicious meal from almost nothing — this is clever and praiseworthy.

On the other end, it sounds suspicious or underhanded — someone is engineering a situation for selfish gain, or forcing something to happen in a way that feels dishonest.

In the middle is a more neutral use — someone simply managed to do something difficult.

The guiding principle is this: the more natural, honest, and effortless something is, the less we use "contrive." The more calculated, forced, or manipulative it is, the more "contrive" fits. The word always carries a hint that human engineering was behind the outcome — whether that engineering is admirable or suspicious depends on context.

You will encounter the adjective contrived very frequently, so you must know it. When something is called contrived, it means it feels forced, artificial, or unnatural — as though it was too obviously engineered rather than arising genuinely.

  • The ending of the film felt contrived — it didn't feel like a natural conclusion; you could sense the writer bending events artificially to wrap things up.
  • His apology seemed contrived — it didn't feel real or spontaneous; it felt rehearsed and calculated.
  • The plot twist was so contrived that nobody believed it.

The core feeling with "contrived" is: this doesn't feel real. Someone tried too hard to make it happen this way. When a story, a situation, an excuse, or an emotion is contrived, it has lost its authenticity because the machinery behind it is showing.

Knowing how "contrive" behaves in a sentence will help you use and recognize it correctly.

Pattern 1 — contrive + to + verb
This is the most common pattern. "She contrived to escape." "He contrived to win." "They contrived to avoid disaster." This pattern covers Senses 1 and 2.

Pattern 2 — contrive + a noun
"She contrived a plan." "He contrived a solution." "They contrived a scheme." Here you are contriving a thing — a plan, a method, a device, a story. This pattern is common for Senses 1 and 3.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close to "contrive," but each has a different flavor.

Plan is completely neutral. It simply means to think ahead. "Contrive" always adds the feeling of cleverness, difficulty, or calculation on top of mere planning.

Devise is the closest synonym to "contrive" in Sense 1. Both mean to figure something out cleverly. However, "devise" is more neutral and professional-sounding. "Contrive" hints more strongly at effort, limited resources, or a somewhat calculated approach.

Scheme is more solidly negative — it almost always implies something dishonest or self-serving. "Contrive" in Sense 3 overlaps with this, but "contrive" can still be neutral or positive in its other senses. "Scheme" almost never is.

Manage (as in "manage to do something") is the closest everyday word to Sense 2 of "contrive." But "managed to" is completely neutral, while "contrived to" hints at more deliberate effort — and sometimes a slightly suspicious flavor of how exactly did they pull that off?

"Contrive" always involves a person deliberately engineering an outcome through clever thought and effort. It can mean thinking up a creative solution, managing to do something difficult, or plotting something manipulative. Whether it sounds impressive or shady depends entirely on the context and what is being contrived. Whatever the use, the word never implies something easy, natural, or accidental — there is always a human mind working hard behind the scenes, calculating how to make something happen.
3471:
Something is contrived when it has been deliberately created or arranged — but the effort and artificiality behind it are too visible. It doesn't feel natural, genuine, or spontaneous. It feels engineered, and you can almost sense the invisible hand that built it.

The key insight: things aren't just made, they're made obviously. The machinery shows when it shouldn't.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine you're watching a movie. Two strangers need to meet, so the writer has one drop a phone, the other pick it up, and they lock eyes — all exactly at the right dramatic moment, scored with romantic music. Nothing about it feels like something that would actually happen. You can feel the writer pushing the characters together. That feeling is what "contrived" captures.

Or imagine a friend gives you an excuse for missing your birthday. Instead of a quick, honest reason, they give you a long, carefully-worded story that sounds suspiciously polished — like they rehearsed it. That too feels contrived.

Three things tend to mark something as contrived:

1. It's too convenient.
The pieces fit together a little too perfectly to be believable. Real life is messy and uneven. When something wraps up too neatly, or a coincidence is too well-timed, it feels manufactured.

2. The effort shows.
Good craftsmanship is invisible — you enjoy the result without thinking about the work. Something contrived is the opposite: the effort bleeds through the surface. You notice someone trying, and that trying ruins the effect.

3. It lacks authenticity.
Whether it's an emotion, a plot twist, a conversation, or a situation — contrived things feel performed rather than real. There's a hollowness to them.

"Contrived" is a critical word. Using it is a polite but clear way of saying something is fake or unconvincing. It's not a brutal insult, but it is a genuine criticism. When a critic calls a film's ending contrived, they mean it fails — not because it's badly filmed, but because it doesn't feel earned or true.

It sits alongside words like forced, artificial, and staged.
Where You'll Commonly See It Used

In stories, films, and books
This is where "contrived" is used most often. A contrived plot is one where events happen not because they make sense in the story's world, but because the writer needed them to happen. A contrived coincidence is one that strains believability. A contrived resolution is an ending that solves everything too easily, without the story earning it.

"The villain's sudden change of heart felt contrived — nothing in the story had prepared us for it."

In real-life situations
A situation can be contrived when someone has set it up in a way that seems natural but isn't. For example, if someone orchestrates a "chance" meeting between two people while pretending it wasn't planned, that situation is contrived.

"The whole thing felt contrived — I later found out she had arranged for us to 'run into' each other."

In excuses and explanations
When someone's excuse sounds too worked-out, too careful, too convenient — it feels contrived.

"His explanation was contrived. It answered every possible objection perfectly, which is exactly why nobody believed it."

In emotions and behavior
When a person's reaction seems performed rather than genuine — when they're acting sad, enthusiastic, or surprised rather than actually feeling it — their response comes across as contrived.

"Her enthusiasm seemed contrived. She said all the right things, but her eyes told a different story."

In dialogue and writing
Dialogue in a novel or script is contrived when characters speak in ways real people never would — when the writer uses their words to deliver information or make a point, rather than speaking as that person would naturally.

"The dialogue was contrived. No one actually talks like that."

It's important to separate "contrived" from just "planned" or "deliberate."

  • A surprise party is planned, but it's not contrived — it works and feels genuine.
  • A well-crafted novel is very deliberately constructed, but not contrived — the author's hand is invisible; you're absorbed in the story.
  • A rehearsed speech is prepared, but not contrived — it still sounds sincere and connects with the audience.

The difference is whether the artificiality shows and whether that showing undermines the effect. Contrived things fail to hide their construction, and that failure makes them feel false.

Understanding nearby words helps sharpen your sense of "contrived":

  • Forced — very close; emphasizes that something was pushed into being unnaturally
  • Artificial — broader; means not natural or genuine (a contrived thing is always artificial)
  • Staged — arranged to look real when it isn't (often used for situations)
  • Labored — implies great effort that shows and makes the result feel stiff
  • Strained — similar to forced; suggests something is being stretched beyond what it naturally is

The opposite of contrived: natural, genuine, organic, spontaneous, authentic.

"Contrived" works as an adjective placed before a noun or after a linking verb:

  • A contrived ending (before a noun)
  • The plot felt contrived. (after a linking verb)
  • The coincidence was too contrived to be believable.
  • The apology sounded contrived.

You can also intensify it: deeply contrived, obviously contrived, painfully contrived.

Contrived describes something that has been artificially arranged or manufactured in a way that feels forced and unnatural — because the effort and planning behind it are too visible, making it seem fake rather than genuine.
3472: Control is about having the power to direct, limit, or manage something — to decide what it does, how much of it exists, or what happens to it. If you have control over something, you are the one steering it, holding it back, or setting the rules for it. Think of it as a leash: control is what keeps something from going wherever it wants on its own.

1. Power or Authority Over Something

The most common meaning: control is the power or authority one person, group, or force has over something or someone else.

  • "The general has control of the army." (He has the authority to direct it.)
  • "She has full control over the project." (It's hers to manage.)
  • "The fire is under control." (People are successfully managing it; it isn't spreading.)
  • "The situation is out of control." (No one is successfully managing it; things are going wrong freely.)

Notice the phrases "under control" and "out of control." These are extremely common and important. Something is "under control" when it has been successfully managed — it isn't causing problems. Something is "out of control" when it is running free, with no one successfully restraining it.

You can have control of something (you possess or manage it) or control over something (you have authority above it and can direct or limit it). These are very close in meaning and often interchangeable.

2. The Process of Keeping Something in Check

Control can also mean the ongoing act or process of limiting, regulating, or preventing something from getting out of hand. Here, it's not about a single person having power — it's about a continuous effort to manage something.

This is very common in compound phrases:

  • Pest control — the ongoing management of insects, rats, or other pests so they don't take over.
  • Flood control — the systems (dams, levees) and efforts used to prevent floodwaters from causing damage.
  • Quality control — the process of checking products or services to make sure they meet a certain standard.
  • Birth control — methods used to limit or prevent pregnancy.
  • Gun control — policies that limit or regulate the ownership and use of firearms.
  • Infection control — practices used to stop diseases from spreading.

In all these cases, "control" describes the management and limitation of something that could become dangerous or excessive if left unchecked.

3. A Specific Measure, Rule, or Mechanism That Regulates Something

Closely related to the above, "control" (and especially its plural, controls) can refer to a specific tool, rule, or measure put in place to keep something in order.

  • "The government introduced new controls on spending." (Rules or limits placed on spending.)
  • "Security controls were tightened at the airport." (Specific security measures.)
  • "Financial controls prevented the fraud from going undetected." (Systems and checks that regulate financial activity.)

Here, a "control" is basically a guardrail — something put in place to ensure things don't go wrong.

4. The Operating Mechanism of a Machine or Vehicle

When you talk about the controls of something — a plane, a car, a machine, a video game — you're referring to the physical instruments, buttons, switches, levers, or interfaces that a person uses to operate it.

  • "The pilot sat down at the controls of the aircraft." (The cockpit instruments and levers used to fly the plane.)
  • "She handed him the controls." (She let him take over the operation.)
  • "The engineer lost the controls during the storm." (He lost his ability to operate the machine.)

A related common phrase: a remote control is a device that lets you operate something (like a TV or a drone) from a distance, without being physically connected to it.

A control can also refer to a single specific knob, button, or lever on a machine:

  • "The volume control is on the right side." (The knob or button that adjusts the volume.)

5. Composure — The Ability to Manage One's Own Emotions or Behavior

Control can refer to a person's inner ability to manage their own feelings, reactions, or behavior. This is often called self-control, but the word "control" alone can carry this meaning too.

  • "She kept her control during the interview, despite being very nervous." (She kept herself composed.)
  • "He lost control and started shouting." (He was no longer able to manage his emotions; he acted on impulse.)
  • "It took all his control not to laugh." (It required great inner discipline to restrain the impulse.)

Here, "control" describes the grip a person has over their own internal impulses, emotions, and reactions. If you have control in this sense, you don't let your feelings dictate your actions. If you lose it, your impulses take over.

6. The Scientific Control (A Baseline for Comparison)

In science and research, a control (also called a control group or control condition) is a standard or baseline group that does not receive the thing being tested. It exists so that researchers can compare what happens with the treatment vs. without it, and know that any difference they see is actually caused by the thing being tested.

  • "In the drug trial, one group received the new medicine and the other served as the control." (The control group received no medicine, or a sugar pill, so scientists could measure the drug's true effect.)
  • "Without a control, you can't know if the results are meaningful." (Without a baseline for comparison, you can't be sure your treatment is actually causing the results.)

The logic: if both the treated group and the control group both improve, maybe neither the drug nor the treatment deserves credit — maybe people just get better on their own. The control lets you separate real effects from coincidence.

These are very commonly used and worth knowing deeply:

  • Under control — Successfully managed; not causing a problem. "Don't worry, everything is under control."
  • Out of control — Not being successfully managed; running free and causing problems. "The party got out of control."
  • In control — Having authority and managing effectively. "Stay calm and in control."
  • Lose control — Either to stop being able to manage a situation, or to stop being able to manage one's own emotions. "The driver lost control of the car." / "He lost control and burst into tears."
  • Take control / Gain control — To begin having authority over something. "She took control of the company after her father retired."
  • Beyond (one's) control — Something you have no power over; something you cannot manage or influence. "The delay was beyond our control."
  • Control freak (informal) — A person who has an excessive need to be in charge of everything and finds it very hard to let others manage things.

It helps to see that all these meanings are really one idea from different angles:

  • When a person has control, they have the power to direct or limit something.
  • When something is under control, the process of managing it is succeeding.
  • When rules are put in place, those controls are the tools of management.
  • When you operate a machine, the controls are the physical means by which you direct it.
  • When you stay composed, your control is your inner power to manage yourself.
  • In science, the control is the baseline that lets you manage what you're measuring.

In every case, the fundamental question is the same: Who or what is directing this? Is it being kept in check? Or is it running free? Control is whatever answers "yes, it's being kept in check."
3473:
To control something means to have the power to decide what it does, how it behaves, or what happens to it. When you control something, you are the one steering it — the outcome depends on your decisions and actions.

Think of a steering wheel. The driver controls the car. The car goes where the driver steers it, stops when the driver brakes, and speeds up when the driver accelerates. The driver has the power to determine what the car does. That relationship — one party having power over another — is exactly what "control" captures.

"Control" as a verb is used in several distinct ways, though the central idea of having power over something runs through all of them.

1. To have authority or power over someone or something

This is the broadest meaning. When you control a person, a place, an organization, or a situation, you have the authority to decide what happens there. Others follow your decisions.

The general controlled the entire army.
That company controls 40% of the global market.
The dictator controlled every aspect of life in the country.

Here, "control" means you are in charge — things go the way you want them to go because you have the power to make it so.

2. To manage or operate a device, system, or process

When you control a machine, a system, or a mechanism, you are the one operating it — making it do what you want. This is a more technical or mechanical use.

This remote control controls the television.
The thermostat controls the temperature in the room.
She controls the entire software system from her computer.
The pilot controls the speed and direction of the aircraft.

Notice that in this meaning, the "controller" does not have to be a person. A device can control another device — a thermostat controls the heater, for example.

3. To hold back, restrain, or keep in check

This is a very common and important use. Here, to control something means to prevent it from becoming too strong, too intense, too wild, or too disruptive. You are keeping it within limits.

Emotions and behaviour:

He struggled to control his anger.
She controlled her fear and kept walking.
Can you please control your dog? It's jumping on everyone.
The teacher asked the students to control themselves.

Fires, crowds, situations:

The firefighters worked for hours to control the blaze.
Police were called in to control the crowd.
The situation quickly became impossible to control.

In these examples, something is at risk of "getting out of hand" — going beyond acceptable limits. To control it is to stop that from happening, or to bring it back within those limits.

4. To limit or prevent something from spreading or growing

This sense is especially common in contexts like disease, economics, crime, or pests — situations where something undesirable is spreading, and needs to be stopped or reduced.

Doctors are trying to control the spread of the infection.
The government introduced new measures to control inflation.
Farmers use pesticides to control insects that damage crops.
The new policy is meant to control illegal immigration.

The idea here is not just restraint but limitation — keeping something within a safe or acceptable boundary, or stopping its growth altogether.

5. To dominate or manipulate (a negative, personal sense)

This use has a distinctly negative tone. When someone controls another person in a relationship, it means they use their power to restrict, manipulate, or dominate that person — often in a harmful way. The other person has little freedom.

He tried to control every aspect of her life.
She realized she was in a controlling relationship.
He controlled his children through fear.

Notice that the word "controlling" (the adjective form) is very commonly used to describe such behaviour in a person.

6. To account for or eliminate outside factors (scientific/academic use)

In research, experiments, or studies, "to control for" something means to deliberately eliminate or account for a factor that might otherwise interfere with your results. This keeps the experiment clean and accurate.

The researchers controlled for age, gender, and income level.
To get reliable results, the experiment controlled for external temperature.

This is a specialised but important use. When scientists say they "controlled for" something, they mean they made sure that factor did not accidentally affect what they were measuring.
A Key Distinction: What Makes "Control" Special

Many words are close to "control" in meaning — manage, direct, regulate, guide, restrain, dominate — but "control" is distinct because it implies direct power over outcomes.

  • Manage suggests you are organising and running something (a team, a project), but it doesn't necessarily mean you have total power. A manager works with people.
  • Direct means you are guiding something in a certain direction, but it feels lighter — more like guidance than authority.
  • Regulate means to impose rules or limits, often from an external authority (a government regulates businesses). It's formal and rule-based.
  • Control is more direct and powerful than all of these. It means what happens is up to you. You decide. The thing or person being controlled does not go against your will.
  • Dominate is stronger than control — it suggests total, often oppressive power. Control can be neutral or positive; dominate almost always sounds forceful or negative.

One of the most important things to understand about "control" is that it always has a direction: someone or something is doing the controlling, and someone or something is being controlled.

  • She controls the company. → She is the one with power; the company is what she directs.
  • He can't control his emotions. → He is trying to be the one in charge; his emotions are what he wants to restrain.
  • This dial controls the volume. → The dial is the mechanism of power; the volume is what changes.

You cannot "control" in an abstract or directionless way. The verb always involves a relationship between the one who has the power and the one that receives the effect of that power.

Interestingly, "control" becomes especially visible in English when it is absent. Notice these common expressions:

  • out of control — when something is behaving in a wild, dangerous, or unpredictable way with no one able to stop it (The fire went out of control.)
  • lose control — when you had control but it slipped away (The driver lost control of the vehicle.)
  • beyond control — when the situation is too powerful for anyone to manage (The storm was beyond anyone's control.)
  • take control — when someone steps in and begins directing a situation (She took control of the meeting.)
  • in control — when someone confidently holds power over a situation (Despite the chaos, he seemed completely in control.)

Understanding these phrases will help you recognise "control" in context even when the verb itself isn't in its simplest form.
Grammar: How "Control" Behaves in a Sentence

"Control" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — it cannot stand alone. You must always say what is being controlled.

✅ She controls the narrative.
✅ They controlled the border.
❌ She controls. (incomplete — controls what?)

Common patterns:

  • Subject + control + noun → He controls the budget.
  • Subject + control + possessive + noun → She couldn't control her tears.
  • Subject + control + object + preposition → Scientists controlled for external variables.

• Base form: control (I control, you control, they control)
  • Third person singular: controls (She controls, he controls, it controls)
  • Past tense: controlled (They controlled the situation.)
  • Past participle: controlled (The disease was controlled.)
  • Present participle / gerund: controlling (He is controlling the drone. / Controlling your emotions is difficult.)

The adjective "controlled" means that something is being carefully managed and not excessive — a controlled explosion, a controlled environment, a controlled response.

The adjective "controlling" (applied to a person) has a negative meaning — it describes someone who tries to dominate or manipulate others.
To control something is to hold the power to decide what it does, how it behaves, or how it develops — whether by directing it, restraining it, limiting it, or operating it.
3474:
Something is controversial when it causes strong disagreement among a significant number of people. It is a topic, idea, person, action, statement, or decision that different people have sharply opposing views about — and those views tend to be deeply held, often emotional, and difficult to resolve.

The word comes from the idea of a controversy, which is essentially a prolonged, serious public dispute. When something is controversial, it sits right at the centre of that dispute.

Think of it this way: if you mention something controversial in a room full of people, you will likely split that room. Some people will strongly agree with it. Others will strongly disagree. And both sides will feel that they are right.

Three things are almost always present when something is controversial:

Strong disagreement. Not everyone has to disagree, but enough people do — and they disagree strongly. A mild difference of opinion is not controversy. Controversy involves real tension.

No universally accepted answer. Controversial topics usually touch on values, beliefs, morals, politics, or deeply personal worldviews. Because different people hold different values, there is often no single "correct" answer that everyone can agree on.

A spark of debate. Controversial things naturally invite argument, discussion, and pushback. They are not quietly ignored — they provoke a reaction.

Controversial does not mean wrong. This is a very important distinction. Saying something is controversial only means it is disputed — not that it is false, harmful, or bad. A scientific finding can be controversial at first and later be proven completely correct. A political policy can be controversial and still be beneficial. The word describes the reaction to something, not its moral value or truthfulness.

Controversy exists on a spectrum. Something can be mildly controversial (a new school policy that some parents dislike) or deeply controversial (a war, a historic injustice, or a law that divides an entire nation). The degree of controversy depends on how many people disagree, how strongly they feel, and how much is at stake.

Controversy is often relative to context. What is controversial in one country, culture, religion, or time period may be completely uncontroversial in another. For example, the idea that women should vote was extremely controversial 150 years ago in many countries. Today, in most parts of the world, it is not controversial at all. This shows that controversy reflects the attitudes and values of a particular group of people at a particular time — not some permanent, universal truth about the topic itself.

A person can be controversial too. When we call someone a "controversial figure," we mean that opinions about them are sharply divided. Some people admire them, others criticise or oppose them, and the disagreement tends to be strong and public. Controversial public figures often include certain politicians, artists, activists, or business leaders whose actions or beliefs provoke strong reactions on both sides.

It helps to understand what the word does not mean:

It does not mean simply "unpopular." Something unpopular is mostly disliked — but controversy requires opposing views, not just negative ones.

It does not mean "offensive" or "inappropriate," though some controversial things can also be offensive. Many controversial topics are perfectly reasonable subjects of debate — they are just unsettled.

It does not mean "rare" or "unusual." A topic can be very common and still be controversial (like debates about taxes, diet, or education).
How It Is Used in Sentences

The adjective "controversial" is placed before a noun or after a linking verb like is, was, seems, or remains:

"The government made a controversial decision to raise taxes." (placed before a noun)

"The new law is deeply controversial." (placed after a linking verb)

"He is one of the most controversial figures in modern politics." (describing a person)

"Her controversial speech sparked protests across the country." (describing something someone said or did)

Certain words appear very naturally alongside "controversial":

"A highly controversial topic" — intensifies the degree of controversy.
"A deeply controversial decision" — suggests the controversy touches something fundamental.
"A controversial figure/person" — someone who divides opinion strongly.
"A controversial statement/remark/claim" — something someone said that sparked disagreement.
"Controversial policies/laws/measures" — decisions that divide public opinion.
"Remain controversial" — used when something has been debated for a long time and is still unresolved.

Disputed — similar to controversial, but more factual. A disputed claim is one where people disagree about whether it is true. Controversial is broader and includes disagreements about values and judgments, not just facts.

Contentious — almost identical in meaning to controversial, but slightly stronger. Contentious suggests the disagreement is more heated and likely to cause conflict or argument. Think of contentious as "controversial with an edge."

Divisive — when something is divisive, it actively splits people into opposing camps. Something divisive causes division. All divisive things tend to be controversial, but not everything controversial is intensely divisive.

Debatable — this means "open to argument." It is softer than controversial. Something debatable is uncertain and can be argued either way, but it doesn't necessarily generate the emotional heat that controversial things do.

Polarising — when something is polarising, people tend to move to extreme opposite positions — strongly for or strongly against, with very little middle ground. Polarising is a specific type of controversial.

The natural opposite of controversial is uncontroversial or non-controversial — meaning something that is widely accepted, agreed upon, and does not generate significant disagreement. You can also use words like settled, accepted, or agreed to convey the same idea depending on context.
A Simple Way to Remember It

If you ever want to check whether a word fits, ask yourself: "Would mentioning this strongly divide people's opinions?" If yes, it is controversial. The heart of the word is this — strong disagreement that refuses to quietly go away.
3475:
A controversy is a prolonged, public disagreement about a topic where people hold strong, opposing opinions and neither side easily backs down. It is not just any disagreement — it is a significant one that tends to involve many people, stirs up strong feelings, and often continues over a long period of time without a clear or quick resolution.

Think of it this way: when a topic is so debatable that it divides people into opposing camps, and those people argue loudly and persistently about it — that situation is a controversy.
Breaking Down What Makes Something a "Controversy"

Not every disagreement qualifies as a controversy. A controversy has a specific character. Understanding its key ingredients will help you use the word precisely.

It involves strong, opposing views. In a controversy, two or more sides exist, and each side genuinely believes it is right. The disagreement is not minor or casual — people feel strongly about it.

It is usually public. A private argument between two friends about what to eat for dinner is not a controversy. A controversy plays out in public — in the news, in politics, in society, on social media, in science, or in culture. Many people are aware of it and many participate in the disagreement.

It is genuinely debatable. A controversy is not simply about something that is factually wrong. If someone claims the sky is green, that is not a controversy — that is just an error. A controversy exists when a topic is complex enough that reasonable, intelligent people can look at it and arrive at genuinely different conclusions. This is a very important distinction.

It tends to be unresolved for a significant time. Controversies are not quick fights. They linger. Sometimes for years, decades, or even longer. This is partly because the topic is hard to resolve, and partly because the feelings involved are deep.

It often carries a sense of heat and tension. The word "controversy" signals that a topic is sensitive, divisive, or emotionally charged. It warns you that people disagree — and disagree intensely.
Everyday Examples to Build Your Intuition

To really feel the word, here are examples across different areas of life.

In politics: The debate over gun control laws has been a long-running controversy in the United States. People on one side argue passionately for stricter laws; people on the other side argue equally passionately against them. No easy answer has resolved it.

In science: When a new study comes out suggesting something surprising — say, that a common food is harmful — it can spark a controversy among scientists and the public if other experts push back and say the evidence is weak.

In entertainment: When a famous singer releases a song that many people find offensive, the public outcry and debate that follows is a controversy. People argue about freedom of expression vs. responsibility.

In sport: When a referee makes a game-changing decision that many believe was wrong, the argument that erupts in the media and among fans is a sports controversy.

Notice that in every case, there are real people disagreeing loudly, the issue is playing out in public, and the disagreement is not immediately resolved.

The word is versatile. Here are the most natural patterns you will encounter.

You can say something causes or sparks or stirs or generates or fuels controversy — all of these mean that something triggered a public disagreement.

"The politician's speech sparked controversy across the country."
"The new policy caused significant controversy."
"His decision stirred controversy among fans."

You can say someone or something is at the center of controversy, or surrounded by controversy, or mired in controversy — these mean that a person or thing is the main subject of a heated public debate, often in a negative way.

"The company found itself at the center of controversy after the scandal broke."
"The director has been surrounded by controversy for years."

You can talk about a controversy over something, or a controversy about something, to specify what the disagreement is about.

"There is a growing controversy over the use of artificial intelligence in schools."
"The controversy about the vaccine policy divided the medical community."

The plural is simply controversies — used when referring to multiple separate disputes.

"The politician was known for his many controversies."
"Scientific history is full of controversies that were eventually resolved."
The Tone and Weight of the Word

"Controversy" is a fairly serious, grown-up word. When you use it, you are signaling that a matter is not trivial — it is something that has genuinely divided people in a meaningful way. It is neutral in itself; it does not automatically take a side. Saying "X is controversial" or "X caused controversy" does not mean X is wrong or right — it simply means X has generated strong, opposing reactions.

This neutrality is important. A journalist might write "the new law has sparked controversy" without telling you whether the law is good or bad. The word is just describing the reaction — the public split — not passing judgment on the topic itself.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Argument refers to a disagreement between specific individuals, usually in a direct exchange. It is personal and often short-lived. A controversy is bigger, more public, and involves many more people.

Debate can be formal and structured, like a planned event where two people argue opposing sides of a topic. Debate can also just mean the general back-and-forth of ideas. Controversy has more emotional heat and tension than debate, and it is less organized.

Dispute often refers to a specific conflict between defined parties — like a legal dispute between two companies. It tends to be more focused and concrete. Controversy is broader and more socially or culturally diffuse.

Scandal involves wrongdoing, moral failure, or shock — it implies someone did something bad. Controversy does not require wrongdoing; it just requires strong disagreement. All scandals tend to produce controversy, but not all controversies are scandals.

Since you are learning the noun, it helps to know how this word family works.

Controversial (adjective) — describing something that causes or is likely to cause controversy. "Abortion is a controversial topic." "It was a controversial decision."

Controversially (adverb) — in a way that causes controversy. "He controversially sided with the opposition."

Uncontroversial (adjective) — the opposite; describing something that most people agree on and that does not generate strong disagreement. "It was an uncontroversial choice."
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you had to boil it down to one sentence: a controversy is a serious, public, ongoing disagreement about a topic where people hold strong opposing views and the matter is genuinely difficult to resolve. It is bigger than a simple argument, more emotionally charged than a debate, and implies that something significant is at stake — enough for many people to care deeply and disagree loudly.
3476:
To controvert something means to argue against it or dispute its truth, typically using reasoning, logic, or evidence. When you controvert a claim, you are not just saying "I disagree" — you are actively taking a stance against it and putting up an argument to challenge it.

Think of it this way: someone puts forward a statement or a position, and you come back with a counter-argument to oppose, deny, or disprove it. That act of reasoned, deliberate opposition is what controvert captures.

Imagine a scientist stands up and says, "This medicine is completely safe." Now, another scientist steps forward and says, "No — here is the data that shows it causes side effects." That second scientist is controverting the first one's claim. They are not just shaking their head — they are actively challenging the statement with substance.

So the word carries two important things at once:

  • Opposition — you are against the claim
  • Active argument — you are doing something about it, not just silently disagreeing
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

This is where precision matters. Several words look similar to controvert in meaning, but they are not the same:

  • Disagree is the broadest and weakest of all. You can disagree with someone simply by feeling differently — no argument needed. Controvert is stronger; it demands that you actually engage and push back with reasoning.
  • Contradict means to say the opposite of what someone has said. It is more about a direct verbal clash — "You said X, I say not-X." Controvert goes further, because it implies you are not just stating the opposite but building a case against the original claim.
  • Refute means to successfully prove something wrong — it implies you have won the argument. Controvert makes no such guarantee. You can controvert a claim and still not fully defeat it. The effort is there; the victory is not promised.
  • Dispute is probably the closest sibling to controvert. Both mean to challenge or contest. However, dispute is more commonly used in everyday language and can apply broadly to disagreements (even personal ones), while controvert tends to be used in more intellectual, academic, or formal contexts — debating ideas, theories, arguments, or positions.

• It does not mean to simply ignore a claim.
  • It does not mean to misunderstand something.
  • It does not mean to prove something wrong with finality (that would be refute).
  • It is not about personal dislike or emotional opposition — controvert is a reasoned, intellectual act.

These examples go from simple to more layered so you can see the full range:

  1. The defense attorney worked hard to controvert the prosecution's evidence. — She was actively challenging and arguing against the evidence in court.
  2. Several economists controverted the government's claim that the policy had no drawbacks. — They disputed the official claim with their own analysis.
  3. No one could successfully controvert his findings, so they were accepted as fact. — People tried to argue against his findings but couldn't pull it off.
  4. The new study controverts what scientists believed for decades. — The study argues against and challenges a long-standing belief.
  5. She published an essay controverting the popular theory that talent alone leads to success. — She built a formal argument against that idea.
The Closely Related Word You Must Know

Since you want to be fully equipped with this word for life, there is one related form you absolutely need:

Incontrovertible (adjective) — This means something that cannot be controverted. It is beyond dispute, beyond argument, beyond challenge. If a fact is incontrovertible, no one can reasonably argue against it.

Example: The video footage was incontrovertible evidence of what had happened. — No one could dispute it.

You will encounter incontrovertible far more often in everyday reading than controvert itself, so knowing the connection between the two gives you a big advantage.

Controvert lives in the world of ideas, arguments, and intellectual debate. It is the word used when scholars, scientists, lawyers, journalists, and thinkers push back against a position with purpose and substance. It signals serious, reasoned opposition — not a squabble, not a gut reaction, but a deliberate challenge to something that has been claimed or believed.

If you ever see a theory, statement, or belief being actively challenged with arguments and evidence, the act of that challenge is controverting.
3477:
Contumacious means stubbornly and boldly refusing to obey authority — not out of confusion or fear, but out of open, defiant contempt.

A contumacious person isn't just breaking a rule. They are deliberately and persistently refusing to follow orders or submit to authority, almost as if they're daring the authority to do something about it. There is an arrogance to it. A swagger of disobedience.

Think of it as three things happening at once:

1. Stubbornness — They won't budge. No matter how many times they are told, warned, or commanded, they hold their ground and refuse.

2. Deliberateness — This is not an accident or a misunderstanding. They know what is being asked of them, and they are choosing, consciously and firmly, to defy it.

3. Contempt — There's a flavour of disrespect in it. A contumacious person isn't quietly slipping away from a rule — they are almost openly scoffing at it and at whoever is enforcing it.

Together, these three give you contumacious: wilfully, stubbornly, and scornfully defiant of authority.
What Makes This Word Special (The Fine Edge)

Many words describe disobedience, but contumacious has a very specific flavour. Let's see how it stands apart:

  • Disobedient is broad and mild — a child who doesn't clean their room is disobedient. That's too weak for contumacious.
  • Rebellious suggests a general spirit of resistance, often against a system. Contumacious is more specific — it's about actively refusing a direct command or authority.
  • Insubordinate is close — refusing the orders of someone above you — but it doesn't carry the same fierce, contemptuous edge.
  • Recalcitrant is perhaps the closest cousin — it also means stubbornly uncooperative. But recalcitrant leans more on unmanageability, while contumacious adds open defiance and scorn on top of that.

So if recalcitrant is a mule that refuses to move, contumacious is a mule that kicks the farmer in the shin while refusing to move.
Where It Is Most at Home

This is a formal, even somewhat elevated word. You won't hear it in casual conversation. It appears most naturally in:

Legal writing and proceedings — This is its most classic home. A defendant who ignores court orders, a witness who flat-out refuses to testify despite a judge's directive, or a party who treats the court's authority with contempt can all be described as behaving in a contumacious manner. Courts can punish contumacious conduct.

Formal writing and literature — In essays, formal criticism, or literary fiction, you might describe a character or historical figure as contumacious when they mount a bold, sustained, scornful refusal to submit to power or law.

Describing people in positions of subordination who defy those above them — A soldier who openly and persistently defies commanding officers. An employee who repeatedly and brazenly refuses to follow management directives not out of confusion but out of purposeful contempt.

Here are examples that show the word at work, so the meaning becomes vivid and locked in:

  • "The contumacious defendant interrupted the judge repeatedly and refused to recognize the court's authority over him."
    → He wasn't confused. He was openly, stubbornly scorning the court.
  • "Despite three written warnings and a formal hearing, the contumacious employee continued to ignore every workplace policy with a kind of proud defiance."
    → Stubborn + deliberate + contemptuous. All three are present.
  • "The young general proved contumacious in the face of orders from high command, convinced that his own judgment was superior."
    → He isn't just disagreeing quietly — he's defiantly refusing to comply.
  • "Her contumacious refusal to cooperate with the investigation led the court to hold her in contempt."
    → Note how naturally this word lives alongside "contempt." They are close relatives in feeling.

When you call someone contumacious, you are not just saying they disobeyed. You are saying something stronger and sharper — that they refused to be controlled, that they met authority with a kind of bold, almost scornful stubbornness. The word carries a sense of severity. It is not a word you use lightly. It suggests that the defiance is persistent, principled in its contempt, and completely deliberate.

It is a word with a hard edge to it — and that hard edge is exactly what makes it precise and irreplaceable in the right context.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Contumacious = stubbornly, deliberately, and contemptuously defiant of authority — refusing to obey not by accident, but with bold, persistent scorn.
3478:
Contumacy means stubborn, willful refusal to obey authority — most often, the authority of a court of law.

When someone commits contumacy, they are not forgetting to comply, not struggling to comply, and not accidentally failing to comply. They are making a firm, conscious, persistent choice to disobey — even though they fully understand what is being demanded of them. That deliberate quality is everything. It is the difference between a person who misses a court date because of a genuine emergency and a person who simply decides not to show up because they refuse to acknowledge the court's power over them. Only the second person is guilty of contumacy.
The Three Qualities That Define It

Three things must be true for something to count as contumacy. First, the disobedience must be willful — a deliberate, knowing choice, not a mistake or misunderstanding. Second, it must be stubborn — not a one-time lapse but a dug-in, persistent resistance. Third, it must be directed at a recognized authority — a court, an institution, or a governing body whose right to give orders is legitimate and established.

Take away any one of these three, and you likely no longer have contumacy.

Contumacy lives almost entirely in legal language, and that is where you need to understand it most clearly. Courts issue orders — to appear and testify, to produce documents, to pay a fine, to stop a certain behavior. When a person receives such an order, understands it, and deliberately ignores or defies it, they have committed contumacy. The law treats this seriously not merely as a broken rule, but as a direct challenge to the authority of the court itself.

Imagine a witness who is legally ordered to appear before a court to give testimony. They receive the summons, read it, understand it, and on the appointed day simply do not show up — not because of illness or emergency, but because they have decided they will not participate. That is contumacy.

These two terms are closely related, and people sometimes confuse them, so it is worth drawing a clear line.

Contempt of court is the broader category. It covers two distinct behaviors: disrespecting or disrupting the court (for example, insulting a judge, behaving outrageously in the courtroom, or interfering with proceedings), and willfully disobeying a court's orders. Contumacy refers specifically and only to that second type — the deliberate non-compliance with orders. So contumacy is a form of contempt, but contempt is not always contumacy. A lawyer who shouts abuse at a judge is in contempt, but that outburst is not contumacy. A defendant who refuses to comply with a court's order is both in contempt and guilty of contumacy.

Though contumacy is overwhelmingly a legal term, it has historically been used outside courtrooms too. In ecclesiastical (church) law, for instance, refusing to obey the lawful authority of church leadership could be labeled contumacy. More loosely, a writer might use the word to describe someone's defiant, unyielding resistance to any legitimate institution or authority — though in everyday writing, such usage is rare and quite formal in tone.

It is worth being precise about the boundaries of this word. Contumacy is not simply disagreeing with an authority or a ruling — you can disagree strongly and still comply. It is not accidental non-compliance, like genuinely forgetting a court date or being too ill to attend. It is not passive ignorance — if a person genuinely never received or understood an order, they cannot technically be guilty of contumacy because the willfulness is absent. And it is not a momentary impulse; the stubborn, persistent quality is essential.

The soul of contumacy is knowing exactly what is demanded of you, having the ability to comply, and choosing, firmly and persistently, not to.

Knowing the related forms will help you recognize this word across contexts. The adjective form is contumacious, used to describe a person or behavior displaying contumacy — you might read of "a contumacious defendant" or "contumacious conduct." The adverb is contumaciously — "she contumaciously refused to produce the documents." And contumaciousness is a noun essentially synonymous with contumacy itself, referring to the general quality or state of being contumacious.

In one sentence: contumacy is the deliberate, stubborn, and persistent defiance of a legitimate authority's orders — most classically, a court's — rooted not in ignorance or inability, but in a willful refusal to submit.
3479:
Contumely means harsh, contemptuous, and humiliating treatment or language directed at someone — the kind that doesn't just insult a person but deliberately degrades them, as if they are beneath the speaker's dignity even to acknowledge as an equal. It is scorn made verbal, or scorn made into an action.

Think of it this way: not all rudeness is contumely. If someone snaps at you because they're having a bad day, that's rudeness. But if someone speaks to you — or treats you — in a way that is designed to make you feel worthless, small, and beneath contempt, that is contumely. There is always an element of superiority and deliberate cruelty in it.
What separates it from similar words

Words like insult, abuse, or mockery are close relatives, but contumely is more specific and more loaded than any of them.

An insult can be casual and momentary — someone calls you a name and moves on. Mockery makes fun of you. Abuse is broadly harmful treatment. But contumely carries a richer and darker flavour: it is contemptuous, it is crushing in tone, and it comes from a place of feeling genuinely superior to the other person. The person dishing out contumely isn't just angry or playful — they look down on you, and they are making sure you feel that.

It is the language of a king dismissing a beggar, a bully humiliating someone they see as powerless, or a powerful official speaking to someone with utter disdain, as though that person has no worth as a human being.

Contumely can appear as words or as actions (or both at once).

As words: openly insulting someone with scorn, calling them names designed not just to offend but to diminish them, speaking about them as though they are beneath serious consideration.

As actions: treating someone with such visible contempt that the treatment itself is a form of degradation — ignoring them pointedly, dismissing them with a wave, humiliating them in front of others, refusing to grant them the basic dignity you'd give a peer.

• The warden treated the prisoners with such contumely that even the guards were uncomfortable.
  • She bore the contumely of her critics with quiet dignity, never once defending herself publicly.
  • The senator's speech was not a debate — it was pure contumely, designed to humiliate rather than persuade.

In each case, notice that the treatment or language is not just negative — it is deliberately contemptuous, loaded with the sense that the person on the receiving end is beneath respect.

Contumely stings in a particular way. Being insulted is unpleasant. Being treated with contumely is crushing — because it attacks not just what you did or said, but your worth as a person. It is belittling with intent. It often leaves the person who receives it feeling publicly shamed, diminished, and stripped of dignity.

This is why the word appears in serious, often dramatic writing. Shakespeare used it famously in Hamlet, where Hamlet lists contumely among the worst pains human beings must silently endure — the arrogant contempt of powerful people directed at those who cannot fight back.
The one-line summary to remember it by

Contumely = deeply contemptuous, humiliating treatment or language that makes a person feel worthless — scorn weaponised.

If you remember that it always involves looking down on someone and making them feel it, you'll never misuse this word.
